claim: Mammalian cells typically start the cell-cycle entry program by activating cyclin-dependent protein kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6).
source: Mammalian cells typically start the cell-cycle entry program by activating cyclin-dependent protein kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle of cell cycle entry.

claim: CDK4/6 activity is clinically relevant as mutations, deletions, and amplifications that increase CDK4/6 activity contribute to the progression of many cancers.
source: CDK4/6 activity is clinically relevant as mutations, deletions, and amplifications that increase CDK4/6 activity contribute to the progression of many cancers.
evidence: This statement is presented in the abstract as established knowledge about the clinical relevance of CDK4/6.

claim: A reporter system was developed to simultaneously monitor CDK4/6 and CDK2 activities in single cells.
source: Here, we developed a reporter system to simultaneously monitor CDK4/6 and CDK2 activities in single cells
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the development of this reporter system as a methodological contribution of the study.

claim: CDK4/6 activity increases rapidly before CDK2 activity gradually increases.
source: we developed a reporter system to simultaneously monitor CDK4/6 and CDK2 activities in single cells and found that CDK4/6 activity increases rapidly before CDK2 activity gradually increases
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract as a result from the reporter system measurements.

claim: CDK4/6 activity can be active after mitosis or inactive for variable time periods.
source: CDK4/6 activity can be active after mitosis or inactive for variable time periods
evidence: This observation is stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Stress signals in G1 can rapidly inactivate CDK4/6 to return cells to quiescence but with reduced probability as cells approach S phase.
source: Markedly, stress signals in G1 can rapidly inactivate CDK4/6 to return cells to quiescence but with reduced probability as cells approach S phase.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a key finding about stress-mediated regulation of CDK4/6.

claim: The study reveals a regulation of G1 length by temporary inactivation of CDK4/6 activity after mitosis.
source: Together, our study reveals a regulation of G1 length by temporary inactivation of CDK4/6 activity after mitosis
evidence: This conclusion is explicitly stated in the abstract as a major finding of the study.

claim: There is a progressively increasing persistence in CDK4/6 activity that restricts cells from returning to quiescence as cells approach S phase.
source: a progressively increasing persistence in CDK4/6 activity that restricts cells from returning to quiescence as cells approach S phase
evidence: This principle is explicitly stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: Mitogens promote entry into the cell cycle in part by inducing the expression of cyclin Ds to activate CDK4 and its paralog CDK6 (CDK4/6).
source: Mitogens promote entry into the cell cycle in part by inducing the expression of cyclin Ds to activate CDK4 and its paralog CDK6 (CDK4/6) (Matsushime et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Matsushime et al., 1994.

claim: A main role of CDK4/6 activation is to phosphorylate retinoblastoma protein (Rb), which is inactivated by hyperphosphorylation on approximately 15 sites.
source: A main role of CDK4/6 activation is to phosphorylate retinoblastoma protein (Rb), which is inactivated by hyperphosphorylation on approximately 15 sites (Dick and Rubin, 2013; Topacio et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dick and Rubin, 2013 and Topacio et al., 2019.

claim: Unphosphorylated or monophosphorylated Rb proteins inhibit chromatin-bound E2F (mostly E2F1-3), repressing the E2F-mediated expression of a large set of cell-cycle regulators including cyclin Es and cyclin As.
source: Unphosphorylated or monophosphorylated Rb proteins inhibit chromatin-bound E2F (mostly E2F1-3), repressing the E2F-mediated expression of a large set of cell-cycle regulators including cyclin Es and cyclin As (Dick and Rubin, 2013; Narasimha et al., 2014; Nevins, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dick and Rubin, 2013; Narasimha et al., 2014; and Nevins, 2001.

claim: When hyperphosphorylated, Rb dissociates from chromatin-bound E2F, promoting entry into the cell cycle by a progressive increase in the activity of CDK2.
source: When hyperphosphorylated, Rb dissociates from chromatin-bound E2F, promoting entry into the cell cycle by a progressive increase in the activity of CDK2 (DeGregori et al., 1995; Spencer et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to DeGregori et al., 1995 and Spencer et al., 2013.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of Rb leads to inactivation of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome-Cdh1 (APC/CCdh1) shortly before cells enter S phase.
source: inactivation of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome-Cdh1 (APC/CCdh1) shortly before cells enter S phase (Cappell et al., 2016; Grant et al., 2018; Ondracka et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cappell et al., 2016; Grant et al., 2018; and Ondracka et al., 2016.

claim: Early studies proposed that CDK4/6 activity may only partially phosphorylates Rb while a CDK2-activity driven positive feedback loop subsequently hyperphosphorylates Rb.
source: Early studies proposed that CDK4/6 activity may only partially phosphorylates Rb while a CDK2-activity driven positive feedback loop subsequently hyperphosphorylates Rb (Geng et al., 1996; Zetterberg et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement describes a hypothesis from earlier studies, supported by citations to Geng et al., 1996 and Zetterberg et al., 1995.

claim: Two studies concluded that CDK4/6 activity only monophosphorylates Rb and E2F targets remain suppressed unless Rb is hyperphosphorylated by CDK2.
source: Two other studies concluded that CDK4/6 activity only monophosphorylates Rb and E2F targets remain suppressed unless Rb is hyperphosphorylated by CDK2 (Narasimha et al., 2014; Sanidas et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement describes conclusions from two studies, supported by citations to Narasimha et al., 2014 and Sanidas et al., 2019.

claim: Mitogens still trigger hyperphosphorylation of Rb in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) where all four cyclin E and A genes were deleted.
source: Our group reported that CDK4/6 activity can be sufficient to hyperphosphorylate Rb in G1, since mitogens still trigger hyperphosphorylation of Rb in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) where all four cyclin E and A genes were deleted.
evidence: This is presented as a finding from the authors' group, demonstrating that CDK4/6 can hyperphosphorylate Rb without cyclin E/A.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of p27 can generate active trimeric CDK4/6 complexes.
source: tyrosine phosphorylation of p27 can generate active trimeric CDK4/6 complexes (Blain, 2008; Guiley et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blain, 2008 and Guiley et al., 2019.

claim: Studies using double p21/p27 and triple p21/27/p57 knockout cells came to different conclusions whether binding of CIP/KIP type CDK inhibitors is required for cells to contain active cyclin D-CDK4/6.
source: but studies using double p21/p27 (Cheng et al., 1999) and triple p21/27/p57 (Tateishi et al., 2012) knockout cells came to different conclusions whether binding of CIP/KIP type CDK inhibitors is required for cells to contain active cyclin D-CDK4/6.
evidence: This statement describes conflicting results from studies cited as Cheng et al., 1999 and Tateishi et al., 2012.

claim: Addition of the cyclin D-CDK4/6 selective inhibitor palbociclib in late G1 caused dephosphorylation of hyperphosphorylated Rb in less than 15 min.
source: Addition of the cyclin D-CDK4/6 selective inhibitor palbociclib in late G1 also caused dephosphorylation of hyperphosphorylated Rb in less than 15 min (Chung et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chung et al., 2019.

claim: An active cyclin D-CDK4 complex with bound tyrosine phosphorylated p27 was unresponsive to palbociclib inhibition.
source: while an active cyclin D-CDK4 complex with bound tyrosine phosphorylated p27 was unresponsive to palbociclib inhibition (Guiley et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guiley et al., 2019.

claim: A nuclear translocation-based reporter was previously developed that can monitor the activation of cyclin E-CDK2 in G1 phase.
source: We previously developed a nuclear translocation-based reporter that can monitor the activation of cyclin E-CDK2 in G1 phase (Hahn et al., 2009; Spencer et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement describes a previous methodological development by the authors, supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2009 and Spencer et al., 2013.

claim: The CDK2 reporter can be phosphorylated in vitro by cyclin E-CDK2 or cyclin A-CDK2 activity.
source: The reporter can be phosphorylated in vitro by cyclin E-CDK2 or cyclin A-CDK2 activity (Spencer et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spencer et al., 2013.

claim: The CDK2 reporter can be phosphorylated by cyclin E/A-CDK1 activity.
source: as well as by cyclin E/A-CDK1 activity (Schwarz et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schwarz et al., 2018.

claim: The CDK2 reporter cannot be phosphorylated by cyclin D-CDK4/6 activity.
source: but not by cyclin D-CDK4/6 activity (Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spencer et al., 2013.

claim: Cyclin E prefers CDK2 over CDK1.
source: Given that cyclin E prefers CDK2 over CDK1 (Koff et al., 1992)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Koff et al., 1992.

claim: Cyclin A typically starts to increase at the G1/S transition.
source: and that cyclin A typically starts to increase at the G1/S transition
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cyclin A expression timing.

claim: There is great variability in the time course of CDK2 activation during G1 between individual cells in the same population.
source: An unexpected result of CDK2 reporter measurements was that there is great variability in the time course of CDK2 activation during G1 between individual cells in the same population (Barr et al., 2017; Schwarz et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barr et al., 2017; Schwarz et al., 2018; and Spencer et al., 2013.

claim: Different cells activate CDK2 activity at different times, or not at all.
source: Different cells activate CDK2 activity at different times, or not at all
evidence: This is stated as an observation from CDK2 reporter measurements.

claim: There is great variation when cells enter S phase.
source: and there is also great variation when cells enter S phase.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from CDK2 reporter measurements.

claim: Mitogen stimulation leads to a gradual increase in cyclin D expression over a period of many hours.
source: Mitogen stimulation leads to a gradual increase in cyclin D expression over a period of many hours (Baldin et al., 1993)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Baldin et al., 1993.

claim: It is often believed that CDK4/6 activation is a main trigger activity for cell-cycle entry in cells exiting quiescence as well as in cycling cells.
source: It is often believed that CDK4/6 activation is a main trigger activity for cell-cycle entry in cells exiting quiescence as well as in cycling cells (Bertoli et al., 2013; Meyerson and Harlow, 1994)
evidence: This statement describes a common belief in the field, supported by citations to Bertoli et al., 2013 and Meyerson and Harlow, 1994.

claim: Recent studies showed that stress signals can reverse cell-cycle entry even after cyclin E-CDK2 has already been activated until APC/CCdh1 is inactivated at the onset of S phase.
source: Most importantly for our study here, recent studies showed that stress signals can reverse cell-cycle entry even after cyclin E-CDK2 has already been activated until APC/CCdh1 is inactivated at the onset of S phase (Cappell et al., 2016; Heldt et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cappell et al., 2016 and Heldt et al., 2018.

claim: The putative CDK4/6 reporter is comprised of a fluorescent protein (mCherry) conjugated to a peptide that contains nuclear import and nuclear export sequences with residues suitable for phosphorylation by CDKs.
source: Specifically, the putative CDK4/6 reporter is comprised of a fluorescent protein (mCherry) conjugated to a peptide that contains nuclear import and nuclear export sequences with residues suitable for phosphorylation by CDKs.
evidence: This describes the design of the CDK4/6 reporter construct.

claim: Relative selectivity for CDK4/6 activity was achieved by adding a cyclin D-CDK4/6-specific docking site fused at the C-terminus.
source: Relative selectivity for CDK4/6 activity was achieved by adding a cyclin D-CDK4/6-specific docking site fused at the C-terminus.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the CDK4/6 reporter.

claim: The CDK4/6-specific docking site is a short C-terminal fragment of Rb (aa 886–928) that has previously been shown to be required for binding of CDK4 to Rb and also required for the phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin D-CDK4 but not by cyclin E-CDK2.
source: The CDK4/6-specific docking site is a short C-terminal fragment of Rb (aa 886–928) that has previously been shown to be required for binding of CDK4 to Rb and also required for the phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin D-CDK4 but not by cyclin E-CDK2 (Topacio et al., 2019; Wallace and Ball, 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Topacio et al., 2019 and Wallace and Ball, 2004, as well as reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The reporter translocated from the nucleus to the cytoplasm before CDK2 activity starts to increase and APC/CCdh1 is inactivated.
source: The reporter translocated from the nucleus to the cytoplasm before CDK2 activity starts to increase and APC/CCdh1 is inactivated (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by references to Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Application of a CDK1 selective inhibitor (RO-3306) did not alter the putative CDK4/6 reporter signal in G1 or S.
source: Application of a CDK1 selective inhibitor (RO-3306) did not alter the putative CDK4/6 reporter signal in G1 or S (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CDK1 inhibitor did not have an effect on the CDK2 reporter in G1 phase.
source: The CDK1 inhibitor also did not have an effect on the CDK2 reporter in G1 phase
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text.

claim: The measured CDK2 signal in G1 is primarily from cyclin E-CDK2, as cyclin A is expected to be degraded in G1 by APC/CCdh1.
source: supporting the previous hypothesis that the measured CDK2 signal in G1 is primarily from cyclin E-CDK2, as cyclin A is expected to be degraded in G1 by APC/CCdh1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Roscovitine has similar inhibitory selectivity for cyclin B-CDK1 and cyclin E/A-CDK2 kinase complexes.
source: We next tested for the relative selectivity of the two reporters using roscovitine, which has similar inhibitory selectivity for cyclin B-CDK1 and cyclin E/A-CDK2 kinase complexes (McClue et al., 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McClue et al., 2002.

claim: CDK2i III (CVT-313) is a kinase inhibitor with a reported 8-fold selectivity for inhibiting cyclin E/A-CDK2 over cyclin B-CDK1.
source: and CDK2i III (CVT-313), a kinase inhibitor with a reported 8-fold selectivity for inhibiting cyclin E/A-CDK2 over cyclin B-CDK1 (Brooks et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brooks et al., 1997.

claim: Addition of CDK2i III and roscovitine significantly suppressed cyclin E-CDK2 activity during G1 phase while also reducing the signal from the putative CDK4/6 reporter by about 10–20% during that time.
source: As expected, addition of CDK2i III and roscovitine significantly suppressed cyclin E-CDK2 activity during G1 phase while also reducing the signal from the putative CDK4/6 reporter by about 10–20% during that time (Figure 1E).
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Each of the three CDK4/6 selective inhibitors nearly fully inhibited the putative CDK4/6 reporter in G1 phase.
source: Conversely, each of the three CDK4/6 selective inhibitors nearly fully inhibited the putative CDK4/6 reporter in G1 phase (Figure 1F).
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Subsets of G1-phase cells slowly reversed the normal steady increase in cyclin E-CDK2 activity following CDK4/6 inhibition.
source: We note that subsets of G1-phase cells slowly reversed the normal steady increase in cyclin E-CDK2 activity following CDK4/6 inhibition
evidence: This observation is stated in the text as a result from the inhibitor experiments.

claim: When CDK4/6 activity is acutely inhibited in S/G2, approximately 35% of the putative CDK4/6 reporter signal cannot be suppressed by the CDK4/6 inhibitors.
source: When CDK4/6 activity is acutely inhibited in S/G2, approximately 35% of the putative CDK4/6 reporter signal cannot be suppressed by the CDK4/6 inhibitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CDK2 activity is likely a main additional contributor to the measured reporter signal at higher levels of CDK2 activity during S and G2 phase.
source: Together, these results suggest that, particularly at higher levels of CDK2 activity during S and G2 phase, CDK2 activity is likely a main additional contributor to the measured reporter signal
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the text based on the inhibitor experiments.

claim: A recent study showed that CDK4/6 activity can still hyperphosphorylate Rb when all cyclin As and Es genes are missing in MEFs.
source: Notably, a recent study by our group showed that CDK4/6 activity can still hyperphosphorylate Rb when all cyclin As and Es genes are missing in MEFs, suggesting that CDK4/6 activity alone can be sufficient for hyperphosphorylating the substrate Rb (Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chung et al., 2019.

claim: The CDK2 reporter signal in MEFs without cyclin E/A was indistinguishable from basal, confirming that the CDK2 reporter signal requires cyclin E or A.
source: After induction of Cre, the CDK2 reporter signal in MEFs without cyclin E/A was, as expected, indistinguishable from basal, confirming that the CDK2 reporter signal requires cyclin E or A (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The putative CDK4/6 reporter signal was still observed in the cyclin E/A knockout MEFs.
source: Importantly, the putative CDK4/6 reporter signal was still observed in the cyclin E/A knockout MEFs
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text.

claim: Acute CDK4/6 inhibition still suppressed the putative CDK4/6 reporter signal in cyclin E/A knockout MEFs.
source: and acute CDK4/6 inhibition still suppressed the putative CDK4/6 reporter signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: CDK4/6 activity alone can generate a CDK4/6 reporter signal, without that E or A type cyclins or CDK2/1 activity are needed for the CDK4/6 reporter signal to increase.
source: Together, these control and knockout measurements argue that CDK4/6 activity alone can generate a CDK4/6 reporter signal, without that E or A type cyclins or CDK2/1 activity are needed for the CDK4/6 reporter signal to increase.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the cyclin E/A knockout experiments.

claim: A corrected CDK4/6 activity can be derived by subtracting a 35% fraction of the CDK2 reporter signal from the simultaneously measured CDK4/6 reporter signal in the same cell.
source: This can be achieved by subtracting a 35% fraction of the CDK2 reporter signal from the simultaneously measured CDK4/6 reporter signal in the same cell to derive a corrected CDK4/6 activity throughout the cell cycle (see Methods).
evidence: This methodological approach is described in the text.

claim: When the correction is applied, the corrected CDK4/6 activity signal can be mostly suppressed upon CDK4/6 inhibition not only in G1 but also in S and G2.
source: When this correction is applied, the corrected CDK4/6 activity signal can be mostly suppressed upon CDK4/6 inhibition not only in G1 but also in S and G2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Materials and method section).
evidence: This result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mitogen stimulation triggers rapid activation of CDK4/6 but only after a 5–13 hr long delay.
source: When revisiting the data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, we can now conclude that mitogen stimulation triggers rapid activation of CDK4/6 but only after a 5–13 hr long delay.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on analysis of the data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 54% of cells persistently increased CDK4/6 activity (CDK4/6high cells) while the remaining cells did not show an increase in CDK4/6 activity (CDK4/6low cells) after mitogen stimulation.
source: When comparing the kinetics of CDK4/6 activation between different cells in the same population after mitogen stimulation, 54% of cells in this experiment persistently increased CDK4/6 activity (CDK4/6high cells) while the remaining cells did not show an increase in CDK4/6 activity (CDK4/6low cells) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This quantitative result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The finding of a rapid increase in CDK4/6 activity after a long delay provides support for a previous hypothesis that CDK4/6 activation might be controlled by an ultrasensitive activation mechanism.
source: The finding of a rapid increase in CDK4/6 activity after a long delay provides support for a previous hypothesis that CDK4/6 activation might be controlled by an ultrasensitive activation mechanism (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: CDK4/6 activity stays persistently high throughout S and G2 phase.
source: Furthermore, while the activity of CDK4/6 rapidly increases to a near maximal level before S-phase, CDK4/6 activity then stays persistently high throughout S and G2 phase as evidenced by cells showing persistent CDK4/6 reporter activity after the APC/CCdh1 degron signal starts to increase (Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by references to multiple figures.

claim: Cyclin D1 is stabilized in G1 by p21.
source: Nevertheless, cyclin D1 is stabilized in G1 by p21 (Chen et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: p21 is degraded in S-phase by Crl4Cdt2.
source: and p21 is degraded in S-phase by Crl4Cdt2 (Abbas et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Abbas et al., 2008.

claim: The low levels of p21 in S-phase may allow for maintenance of CDK4/6 activity at a lower cyclin D level.
source: The low levels of p21 in S-phase may then allow for maintenance of CDK4/6 activity at a lower cyclin D level, providing a potential explanation how CDK4/6 activity can stay elevated in S phase.
evidence: This is presented as a potential explanation based on the observations about p21 and cyclin D.

claim: Previous studies showed that CDK2 reporter analysis can distinguish three paths in cells exiting mitosis: cells can immediately increase CDK2 activity (CDK2inc cells) or cells keep CDK2 activity persistently low (CDK2low cells).
source: Previous studies showed that CDK2 reporter analysis can distinguish three paths in cells exiting mitosis: cells can immediately increase CDK2 activity (CDK2inc cells) or cells keep CDK2 activity persistently low (CDK2low cells) (Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Spencer et al., 2013.

claim: In a third path, cells first keep CDK2 activity low at mitosis exit and then increased CDK2 activity again after a variable delay (CDK2delay cells).
source: In a third path, cells first keep CDK2 activity low at mitosis exit and then increased CDK2 activity again after a variable delay (CDK2delay cells) (Arora et al., 2017; Barr et al., 2017; Moser et al., 2018; Schwarz et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A subset of cells had continuously active CDK4/6 (CDK4/6high cells) starting at the end of mitosis and these cells corresponded to the CDK2inc cells.
source: When we aligned asynchronously cycling cells by the end of mitosis (anaphase), a subset of cells had continuously active CDK4/6 (CDK4/6high cells) starting at the end of mitosis and these cells corresponded to the CDK2inc cells (Figure 3A, left).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Another subset of cells had low CDK4/6 activity at mitotic exit and some of these cells kept CDK4/6 activity persistently off after mitosis, corresponding to CDK2low cells that exit to quiescence.
source: Another subset of cells had low CDK4/6 activity at mitotic exit and some of these cells kept CDK4/6 activity persistently off after mitosis, corresponding to CDK2low cells that exit to quiescence
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: A third subset of cells had first CDK4/6 activity below the threshold and increased CDK4/6 above the threshold typically before 10 hr after mitosis (CDK4/6delay cells), corresponding to CDK2delay cells.
source: A third subset of cells had first CDK4/6 activity below the threshold and increased CDK4/6 above the threshold typically before 10 hr after mitosis (CDK4/6delay cells) (Figure 3A, top left), corresponding to CDK2delay cells.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Cells that persistently activate CDK4/6 also activated CDK2 and inactivated APC/CCdh1 when cells exit mitosis.
source: Consistent with cells entering the cell cycle from quiescence, cells that persistently activate CDK4/6 also activated CDK2 and inactivated APC/CCdh1 when cells exit mitosis (Figure 3A, middle and bottom left).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: A histogram analysis of CDK activities at mitotic exit showed CDK4/6 reaching a maximum activity 2 hr after mitosis, whereas CDK2 activity gradually increased.
source: A histogram analysis of CDK activities at mitotic exit showed CDK4/6 reaching a maximum activity 2 hr after mitosis, whereas CDK2 activity gradually increased (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This analysis result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: CDK4/6 activity stays maximal when cells start DNA replication, while CDK2 activity starts elevated and then keeps gradually increasing before and after S-phase entry.
source: Furthermore, CDK4/6 activity stays maximal when cells start DNA replication, while CDK2 activity starts elevated and then keeps gradually increasing before and after S-phase entry (Figure 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by references to figures.

claim: CDK4/6 activity in MCF10A cells can generally be considered at a given time in the cell cycle to be either in an 'on' or 'off' state both in cycling cells as well as in cells coming out of quiescence while CDK2 activity is gradually increasing throughout G1, S, and G2 phases.
source: Thus, CDK4/6 activity in MCF10A cells can generally be considered at a given time in the cell cycle to be either in an 'on' or 'off' state both in cycling cells as well as in cells coming out of quiescence while CDK2 activity is gradually increasing throughout G1, S, and G2 phases.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the observations of CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity patterns.

claim: Previous studies have shown that cycling cells that exit mitosis have a bimodal distribution in Rb hyperphosphorylation.
source: Previous studies have shown that cycling cells that exit mitosis have a bimodal distribution in Rb hyperphosphorylation (Cappell et al., 2016; Moser et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Rb phosphorylation at Serine 807/811 shows a bimodal distribution and is correlated with activation of E2F transcription targets.
source: As a marker of hyperphosphorylated Rb, we measured Rb phosphorylation at Serine 807/811, which shows a bimodal distribution and is correlated with activation of E2F transcription targets (Cappell et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cappell et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2019; and Yang et al., 2017.

claim: The fraction of cells that has active CDK4/6 and increasing CDK2 activity after mitosis closely matches the fraction of cells with phosphorylated Rb.
source: we found that the fraction of cells that has active CDK4/6 and increasing CDK2 activity after mitosis closely matches the fraction of cells with phosphorylated Rb (Figure 3C)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The CDK4/6high versus CDK4/6low population remains closely correlated over time with whether Rb is phosphorylated for the measured 12 hr period after mitosis.
source: This analysis confirmed that the CDK4/6high versus CDK4/6low population remains closely correlated over time with whether Rb is phosphorylated for the measured 12 hr period after mitosis (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3D,E.

claim: The percent of cells in a population that re-enter or exit the cell cycle after mitosis, or have a delayed cell-cycle entry path with variable G1, were previously shown to vary between different cell types and mitogen and stress stimulation conditions in culture.
source: The percent of cells in a population that re-enter or exit the cell cycle after mitosis, or have a delayed cell-cycle entry path with variable G1, were previously shown to vary between different cell types and mitogen and stress stimulation conditions in culture (Cappell et al., 2016; Moser et al., 2018; Schwarz et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: An analysis of CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity changes after mitosis in RPE1 cells showed a similar bimodal behavior as in MCF10A cells with cells either having active CDK4/6 followed by CDK2 activation, or inactive CDK4/6 without that CDK2 is activated.
source: An analysis of CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity changes after mitosis in RPE1 cells showed a similar bimodal behavior as in MCF10A cells with cells either having active CDK4/6 followed by CDK2 activation, or inactive CDK4/6 without that CDK2 is activated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib abolished both CDK4/6 and CDK2 reporter signals after mitosis in RPE1 cells.
source: Treatment with the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib also abolished both CDK4/6 and CDK2 reporter signals after mitosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This experimental result is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells with high CDK4/6 activity and increasing CDK2 activity at mitotic exit also have Rb hyperphosphorylated which in turn directs cells to rapidly re-enter the cell cycle after a short G1.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that cells with high CDK4/6 activity and increasing CDK2 activity at mitotic exit also have Rb hyperphosphorylated which in turn directs cells to rapidly re-enter the cell cycle after a short G1.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the combined observations.

claim: Cells with low CDK4/6 activity at mitotic exit keep CDK2 activity off and Rb dephosphorylated and exit to quiescence, or alternatively, cells can again rapidly increase CDK4/6 activity after a variable delay of low CDK4/6 activity and enter the next cell cycle, thereby generating G1 lengths of variable duration.
source: Alternatively, cells with low CDK4/6 activity at mitotic exit keep CDK2 activity off and Rb dephosphorylated and exit to quiescence, or alternatively, cells can again rapidly increase CDK4/6 activity after a variable delay of low CDK4/6 activity and enter the next cell cycle, thereby generating G1 lengths of variable duration.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the combined observations.

claim: Previous studies showed that cell-cycle entry can be reversed in G1 by different types of stresses even after CDK2 starts to increase - as long as cells have not yet inactivated APC/CCdh1.
source: Previous studies showed that cell-cycle entry can be reversed in G1 by different types of stresses even after CDK2 starts to increase - as long as cells have not yet inactivated APC/CCdh1 (Cappell et al., 2016; Heldt et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cappell et al., 2016 and Heldt et al., 2018.

claim: For both H2O2 and tunicamycin, a subset of cells in G1 inactivated CDK4/6 activity and reversed cell-cycle entry.
source: For both types of stresses, a subset of cells in G1 inactivated CDK4/6 activity and reversed cell-cycle entry (Figure 4A).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The outcome whether cells will inactivate CDK4/6 and exit the cell cycle was closely correlated with the level of CDK2 activity when stress signals were applied.
source: Intriguingly, the outcome whether cells will inactivate CDK4/6 and exit the cell cycle was closely correlated with the level of CDK2 activity when stress signals were applied (Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Cells having lower CDK2 activity were more likely to inactivate CDK4/6 and exit to quiescence after addition of stress signals while the probability became progressively lower as CDK2 activity increased.
source: Cells having lower CDK2 activity were more likely to inactivate CDK4/6 and exit to quiescence after addition of stress signals while the probability became progressively lower as CDK2 activity increased.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: There was no correlation between the amplitude of the acute CDK4/6 reporter signal and cell-cycle exit.
source: In contrast, there was no correlation between the amplitude of the acute CDK4/6 reporter signal and cell-cycle exit, likely since the CDK4/6 reporter signals were high but had typically plateaued out before stress application (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nearly all cells that already entered S phase and had high CDK2 activity (CDK2 >1.0) did not respond to H2O2 or tunicamycin.
source: Consistent with a correlation between G1 and S progression and stress-mediated reversal, nearly all cells that already entered S phase and had high CDK2 activity (CDK2 >1.0) did not respond to H2O2 or tunicamycin (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by references to figures.

claim: As cells progress in G1 towards S phase, the probability for an individual cell to inactivate CDK4/6 and CDK2 and exit the cell cycle in response to stress progressively decreases until the G1/S transition and then stays low during S phase.
source: Thus, as cells progress in G1 towards S phase, the probability for an individual cell to inactivate CDK4/6 and CDK2 and exit the cell cycle in response to stress progressively decreases until the G1/S transition and then stays low during S phase.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the stress response observations.

claim: Both H2O2 and tunicamycin inactivated CDK4/6 before CDK2 activity started to decrease.
source: When comparing the relative kinetics of CDK4/6 and CDK2 inactivation, both H2O2 and tunicamycin inactivated CDK4/6 before CDK2 activity started to decrease (Figure 4D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4D.

claim: H2O2 inactivated CDK4/6 activity only in CDK2low cells, whereas tunicamycin inactivated CDK4/6 both in CDK2low and CDK2inc cells.
source: Notably, H2O2 inactivated CDK4/6 activity only in CDK2low cells, whereas tunicamycin inactivated CDK4/6 both in CDK2low and CDK2inc cells (Figure 4A,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by references to figures.

claim: All stress and TGF-β1 signaling were more likely to reverse cell-cycle entry in cells having lower CDK2 activity.
source: Similar as H2O2 and tunicamycin, all stress and TGF-β1 signaling were more likely to reverse cell-cycle entry in cells having lower CDK2 activity (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by references to figures.

claim: NaCl rapidly suppressed CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity at a similar rate.
source: While NaCl rapidly suppressed CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity at a similar rate
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: All other stresses and TGF-β1 signaling first inactivated CDK4/6 before CDK2.
source: all other stresses and TGF-β1 signaling first inactivated CDK4/6 before CDK2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The typically more rapid stress-mediated inactivation of CDK4/6 is likely functionally relevant for the subsequent CDK2 inactivation as CDK4/6 activity is still needed to sustain the CDK2 activity increase throughout G1 phase until Rb hyperphosphorylation becomes independent of CDK4/6 activity at the onset of S phase.
source: The typically more rapid stress-mediated inactivation of CDK4/6 is likely functionally relevant for the subsequent CDK2 inactivation as CDK4/6 activity is still needed to sustain the CDK2 activity increase throughout G1 phase (Figure 1D) until Rb hyperphosphorylation becomes independent of CDK4/6 activity at the onset of S phase (Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1D and a citation to Chung et al., 2019.

claim: Stress and inhibitory signals generally act by first inhibiting CDK4/6 activity which in turn suppresses CDK2 activity.
source: Together, our results are consistent with the interpretation that stress and inhibitory signals generally act by first inhibiting CDK4/6 activity which in turn suppresses CDK2 activity
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the stress response observations.

claim: CDK4/6 is in G0/G1 not only rapidly regulated by mitogens but also by stress.
source: arguing that CDK4/6 is in G0/G1 not only rapidly regulated by mitogens but also by stress.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the combined observations of mitogen and stress responses.

claim: There is a progressive persistence in CDK4/6 activity in response to stress as cells approach the G1/S transition.
source: Importantly, there is a progressive persistence in CDK4/6 activity in response to stress as cells approach the G1/S transition.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the stress response observations.

claim: The CDK4/6 reporter is based on a cyclin D-CDK4/6-specific kinase binding site derived from Rb.
source: Our study reports the design of a CDK4/6 activity reporter based on a cyclin D-CDK4/6-specific kinase binding site derived from Rb (Topacio et al., 2019; Wallace and Ball, 2004)
evidence: This statement describes the design of the reporter and is supported by citations to Topacio et al., 2019 and Wallace and Ball, 2004.

claim: The CDK4/6 reporter is based on a modular strategy to develop protein kinase reporters.
source: and a modular strategy to develop protein kinase reporters (Regot et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement describes the design strategy and is supported by a citation to Regot et al., 2014.

claim: The CDK4/6 reporter is best used as a dual reporter together with a CDK2 reporter to subtract a CDK2 contribution from the CDK4/6 reporter signal.
source: We show that the CDK4/6 reporter is best used as a dual reporter together with a CDK2 reporter to subtract a CDK2 contribution from the CDK4/6 reporter signal.
evidence: This recommendation is stated in the text based on the characterization of the reporter.

claim: The corrected CDK4/6 reporter signal stays elevated in mitogen-stimulated cells after cells enter S phase.
source: The corrected CDK4/6 reporter signal stays elevated in mitogen-stimulated cells after cells enter S phase
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: The corrected CDK4/6 reporter signal can be inhibited during S and G2 by CDK4/6-selective inhibitors.
source: and can be inhibited during S and G2 by CDK4/6-selective inhibitors
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: Cells activate CDK4/6 in G1 and can then keep CDK4/6 active throughout the cell cycle.
source: suggesting that cells activate CDK4/6 in G1 and can then keep CDK4/6 active throughout the cell cycle.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the reporter measurements.

claim: A previous study calibrated nuclear cyclin D1 and p21 expression levels and showed that only cells with at least a small excess of nuclear cyclin D1 over p21 after mitosis have Rb hyperphosphorylated while cells with more p21 than cyclin D1 had Rb invariably dephosphorylated.
source: A previous study by our group calibrated nuclear cyclin D1 and p21 expression levels and showed that only cells with at least a small excess of nuclear cyclin D1 over p21 after mitosis have Rb hyperphosphorylated while cells with more p21 than cyclin D1 had Rb invariably dephosphorylated (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: A competition between cyclin D1 and p21 makes it possible for a gradual increase in the relative level of cyclin D1 versus p21 to trigger a rapid activation of CDK4/6 once cyclin D1 exceeds the level of p21.
source: One interpretation of this result was that a competition between cyclin D1 and p21 makes it possible for a gradual increase in the relative level of cyclin D1 versus p21 to trigger a rapid activation of CDK4/6 once cyclin D1 exceeds the level of p21.
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of previous results.

claim: The CDK4/6 reporter signal typically increased rapidly after an often very long variable delay both in cells exiting quiescence and in cells exiting from a transient period of low CDK4/6 activity after mitosis.
source: In support of a hypothesis that CDK4/6 can be activated in an ultrasensitive, bimodal manner, we found that the CDK4/6 reporter signal typically increased rapidly after an often very long variable delay both in cells exiting quiescence and in cells exiting from a transient period of low CDK4/6 activity after mitosis.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text as supporting evidence for ultrasensitive activation.

claim: Previous studies of MCF10A and other cell types showed that cells in the same population have Rb typically either hyperphosphorylated or dephosphorylated after mitosis with the percent of cells having Rb hyperphosphorylated being regulated by mitogen and stress signaling and also differ between cell types.
source: Previous studies of MCF10A and other cell types further showed that cells in the same population have Rb typically either hyperphosphorylated or dephosphorylated after mitosis with the percent of cells having Rb hyperphosphorylated being regulated by mitogen and stress signaling and also differ between cell types (Cappell et al., 2016; Moser et al., 2018; Schwarz et al., 2018; Spencer et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In cells with hyperphosphorylated Rb at mitotic exit, the activity of CDK2 was shown to immediately increase and cells entered the next S phase a few hours later, while cells with low Rb phosphorylation kept their CDK2 activity low after mitosis and cells had either a variable G1 length or they exited to quiescence.
source: In cells with hyperphosphorylated Rb at mitotic exit, the activity of CDK2 was shown to immediately increase and cells entered the next S phase a few hours later, while cells with low Rb phosphorylation kept their CDK2 activity low after mitosis and cells had either a variable G1 length or they exited to quiescence.
evidence: This statement describes previous findings about the relationship between Rb phosphorylation and CDK2 activity.

claim: The bimodal hyperphosphorylation of Rb and bimodal CDK2 activation can be explained by an underlying bimodality in CDK4/6 activity at mitotic exit.
source: Our study here shows that the bimodal hyperphosphorylation of Rb and bimodal CDK2 activation can be explained by an underlying bimodality in CDK4/6 activity at mitotic exit.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the current study's findings.

claim: Cells choose between three paths when they exit mitosis: In one subset of cells, cells keep CDK4/6 active and Rb hyperphosphorylated as cells exit anaphase and mitosis and these cells are characterized by an immediate increase in CDK2 activity and a short G1 length.
source: Together with previous results, our measurements with the CDK4/6 reporter support the hypothesis that cells choose between three paths when they exit mitosis: In one subset of cells, cells keep CDK4/6 active and Rb hyperphosphorylated as cells exit anaphase and mitosis and these cells are characterized by an immediate increase in CDK2 activity and a short G1 length.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the combined observations.

claim: A second subset of cells have CDK4/6 activity low and Rb dephosphorylated at mitotic exit and CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity then stay persistently low until cells enter quiescence or a postmitotic state.
source: A second subset of cells have CDK4/6 activity low and Rb dephosphorylated at mitotic exit and CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity then stay persistently low until cells enter quiescence or a postmitotic state.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the combined observations.

claim: A third subset of cells start the same way with CDK4/6 and CDK2 being inactive and Rb dephosphorylated after mitosis, but after a variable delay, these cells will again increase CDK4/6 activity, hyperphosphorylate Rb, and increase CDK2 activity to re-enter the next cell cycle.
source: A third subset of cells start the same way with CDK4/6 and CDK2 being inactive and Rb dephosphorylated after mitosis, but after a variable delay, these cells will again increase CDK4/6 activity, hyperphosphorylate Rb, and increase CDK2 activity to re-enter the next cell cycle.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the combined observations.

claim: Several previous studies have shown that G1 is the most variable phase of the cell cycle and regulation of G1 length is important to regulate cell differentiation.
source: Several previous studies have shown that G1 is the most variable phase of the cell cycle and regulation of G1 length is important to regulate cell differentiation (Lange and Calegari, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lange and Calegari, 2010.

claim: Cells can control G1 length and cell-cycle duration in part by switching CDK4/6 activity off for a variable time period after mitosis.
source: Our study thus suggests that cells can control G1 length and cell-cycle duration in part by switching CDK4/6 activity off for a variable time period after mitosis.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the study's findings.

claim: CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity become progressively more resistant to stress as cells approach S phase.
source: Our study further shows that CDK4/6 and CDK2 activity become progressively more resistant to stress as cells approach S phase.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text based on the stress response experiments.

claim: Previous studies showed that stress can trigger cell-cycle exit in G1 until the onset of S phase.
source: While previous studies showed that stress can trigger cell-cycle exit in G1 until the onset of S phase (Cappell et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cappell et al., 2016.

claim: Stress-mediated inactivation of CDK2 becomes less effective towards the onset of S phase.
source: and that stress-mediated inactivation of CDK2 becomes less effective towards the onset of S phase (Heldt et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Heldt et al., 2018.

claim: Most stresses trigger first a rapid inactivation of CDK4/6 and that the loss in CDK4/6 activity is then followed by a reduction in CDK2 activity and exit to quiescence.
source: We measured the response to a number of different types of stress signals and showed that most trigger first a rapid inactivation of CDK4/6 and that the loss in CDK4/6 activity is then followed by a reduction in CDK2 activity and exit to quiescence.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on the stress response experiments.

claim: CDK2 activity and cell-cycle entry remain sensitive to acute inhibition by the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib until the end of G1.
source: This is also consistent with CDK2 activity and cell-cycle entry remaining sensitive to acute inhibition by the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib until the end of G1 (Chung et al., 2019).

claim: CDK4/6 activity becomes increasingly more resistant to stress towards the end of G1.
source: We further show that CDK4/6 activity becoming increasingly more resistant to stress towards the end of G1.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text based on the stress response experiments.

claim: Such a hysteresis in CDK4/6 activity in response to stress was unexpected since the switch-mechanism driving cell-cycle entry is typically believed to self-reinforce Rb hyperphosphorylation and CDK2 activity.
source: Such a hysteresis in CDK4/6 activity in response to stress was unexpected since the switch-mechanism driving cell-cycle entry is typically believed to self-reinforce Rb hyperphosphorylation and CDK2 activity.
evidence: This statement presents the finding as unexpected based on current understanding.

source: MCF10A human mammary epithelial cells (ATCC, CRL-10317) were cultured in phenol red-free DMEM/F12 (Invitrogen) supplemented with 5% horse serum, 20 µg/ml EGF, 10 µg/ml insulin, 0.5 µg/ml hydrocortisone, 100 ng/ml cholera toxin, 50 U/ml penicillin, and 50 µg/ml streptomycin.

source: The live-cell CDK4/6 reporter was cloned into a pLenti vector using the Gibson cloning method to assemble fragments of mCherry, a peptide containing a bipartite nuclear localization sequence (bNLS) and a nuclear export sequence (NES), and the C-terminus of Rb containing amino acids 886–928 (pLenti-mCherry-CDK4KTR).

source: As added notes, we had difficulties constructing responsive CDK4/6 reporters when replacing mCherry with different fluorescent proteins. This may suggest that mCherry conjugating contributes to an optimal performance of the CDK4/6-regulated import-export regulation.

source: Also, due to higher stability of mCherry in low pH compared to other reporters, the CDK4/6 reporter can accumulate in lysosomes for some experimental conditions, which can add a background cytoplasmic signal in the ratio-analysis.

source: Cells were fixed by adding 4% paraformaldehyde at a ratio of 1:1 to culture medium (final 2% paraformaldehyde) for 15 min.

claim: Multiplication of a correction factor of approximately 0.35 to the measured CDK2 activity results in a near constant derived reporter signal during the cell cycle after CDK4/6 inhibition.
source: To calculate the contribution of CDK2 activity to the CDK4/6 reporter in S/G2 phase, we used CDK4/6 inhibition and linear regression. This analysis showed that multiplication of a correction factor of approximately 0.35 to the measured CDK2 activity results in a near constant derived reporter signal during the cell cycle after CDK4/6 inhibition.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating the corrected CDK4/6 activity.

claim: Corrected CDK4/6 activity = CDK4/6 reporter activity - 0.35*CDK2 reporter activity.
source: Corrected CDK4/6 activity = CDK4/6 reporter activity - 0.35*CDK2 reporter activity.
evidence: This is the formula for calculating corrected CDK4/6 activity.
